concept.name: DNS & Traffic Routing

relationships.description: Connects DNS & Traffic Routing to api gateway in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: DNS and traffic routing map human-readable hostnames to optimal, healthy server IPs using hierarchical caching, Anycast BGP, health checks, and geo/latency-aware policies.
spark.keyTakeaway: DNS is a pull-based, heavily cached control plane—even with a 30 s TTL, stubborn OS, browser, and JVM caches make instant DNS-only failover impossible without Anycast or edge proxies.

concept.whyItMatters: DNS is the first network hop for virtually every user request. Misconfigured TTLs, missing apex records, or naive round-robin DNS can route European users to US-West servers, pin traffic to dead regions for hours after an outage, or overwhelm a backup cluster during failover.
whenToUse: Steering global users to the closest healthy regional load balancer via latency-based or GeoDNS policies.
Performing gradual blue/green traffic shifts or weighted canary rollouts (e.g., 95% v1 / 5% v2) across independent clusters.
Implementing multi-cloud or multi-region disaster recovery failover when an entire cloud region goes dark.
whenNotToUse: Sub-second per-request load balancing or instant connection draining across backend pods (use L4/L7 proxies like Envoy, HAProxy, or ALB).
Fine-grained A/B testing or user-session stickiness (DNS sees the recursive resolver's IP, not individual browser sessions).
Enforcing instant emergency cutovers if clients are legacy JVMs or IoT devices that ignore low TTLs.
keyPoints: Standard DNS runs over UDP port 53 (512-byte classic limit, raised to 1232–4096 bytes via EDNS0) with TCP fallback for large responses/DNSSEC; DoT (port 853) and DoH (port 443) encrypt queries.
**Anycast BGP** announces the same IP prefix from dozens of edge POPs worldwide so BGP routes users to the topologically nearest edge, while **GeoDNS/Latency DNS** returns different IPs per region.

**EDNS Client Subnet (ECS, RFC 7871)** forwards a truncated client `/24` IPv4 or `/56` IPv6 prefix from the recursive resolver to the authoritative DNS server so GeoDNS routes to the user's region, not the resolver's.
RFC 1034 forbids a `CNAME` at the zone apex (`example.com`) alongside `SOA`/`NS` records; providers work around this with `ALIAS` / `ANAME` / CNAME flattening.
Negative caching (`NXDOMAIN`) is governed by the `SOA` record's minimum TTL field—a high SOA minimum can prolong an outage long after a deleted record is restored.

examples.title: Regional Failover with Route 53 Health Checks
examples.scenario: An application runs active-active in `us-east-1` and `eu-west-1` behind latency-based DNS (`TTL = 60 s`) with HTTPS health checks polling `/healthz` every `30 s`.
examples.outcome: When `us-east-1` fails 3 consecutive health checks (90 s), Route 53 stops returning the US ALB IP and routes new DNS queries to `eu-west-1` while existing clients drain over 1–3 minutes.

examples.title: Anycast Edge + Origin Shielding on Cloudflare
examples.scenario: A global SaaS exposes `api.example.com` via Anycast BGP across 300+ edge POPs instead of exposing regional origin IPs directly in DNS.
examples.outcome: Every user hits a local edge POP in <20 ms for TLS termination, and origin failover happens over private/backbone health checks in <5 seconds without waiting for client DNS TTLs to expire.

tradeOffs.factor: Low DNS TTL (30–60 s) vs. High DNS TTL (3600–86400 s)
tradeOffs.pro: Low TTLs allow faster traffic shifts during regional outages or migrations.
tradeOffs.con: Low TTLs increase recursive lookup frequency (adding 20–100 ms cold-lookup latency), raise authoritative DNS query bills, and fail open if the authoritative provider suffers an outage.

tradeOffs.factor: Anycast BGP Edge vs. GeoDNS / Latency-Based DNS
tradeOffs.pro: Anycast enables sub-second edge routing and DDoS absorption at a single static IP with zero client-cache staleness.
tradeOffs.con: BGP routing changes can theoretically reset long-lived TCP connections mid-flight, and operating global Anycast requires an ASN and multi-POP edge presence (or a CDN).

tradeOffs.factor: DNS-Level Weighted Routing vs. L7 Gateway Canary
tradeOffs.pro: Weighted DNS splits traffic across completely separate cloud providers or regions with zero shared proxy hop.
tradeOffs.con: Because corporate NATs and public resolvers cache answers per resolver, a 5% DNS weight can actually send 20% of real user traffic if a large ISP hits the canary record.

failureModes.name: Stubborn Client & JVM DNS Pinning
failureModes.description: Older or misconfigured JVMs cache DNS forever (`networkaddress.cache.ttl=-1` when SecurityManager is active) or OS/ISP resolvers clamp minimum TTLs to 300 s, sending traffic to a dead IP.
failureModes.mitigation: Explicitly set `-Dsun.net.inetaddr.ttl=30` in JVM services, front origins with Anycast edge proxies, and keep old IPs draining gracefully.

failureModes.name: Cascading Failover Overload
failureModes.description: Region A fails and DNS shifts 100% of Region A's traffic to Region B, which is only provisioned for 60% headroom, crashing Region B too.
failureModes.mitigation: Pre-provision N+1 failover capacity, apply progressive load shedding at Region B's ingress, or split failover across multiple healthy regions.

failureModes.name: Missing EDNS Client Subnet (ECS) Misrouting
failureModes.description: A user in Mumbai uses a privacy-focused resolver that strips ECS; the authoritative server sees an out-of-region resolver IP and routes the user to Frankfurt.
failureModes.mitigation: Use Anycast BGP at the edge (which routes by the user's actual IP packet, independent of DNS resolver location) or deploy regional edge POPs.

failureModes.name: NXDOMAIN Negative Caching Outage
failureModes.description: A Terraform typo briefly deletes `api.example.com` for 20 seconds. Resolvers cache `NXDOMAIN` for the `SOA` minimum TTL (e.g., 3600 s), keeping users down for an hour after the fix.
failureModes.mitigation: Keep the `SOA` minimum/negative-caching TTL low (60–300 s) and protect critical DNS records with change-approval gates.

commonMistakes: Attempting to create a `CNAME` record at the root/apex domain (`example.com`), breaking `MX` and `NS` resolution instead of using `ALIAS`/`ANAME` flattening.
Setting a `0 s` or `5 s` DNS TTL expecting instant failover, while ignoring ISP minimum-TTL clamping and browser connection pooling.
Pointing a health check at a shallow `/ping` endpoint that returns `200 OK` even when the region's database is down, leaving DNS routing into a broken region.
Using DNS round-robin without active health checks, causing 50% of users to hang on TCP timeouts when one server dies.
Forgetting to lower TTLs from `3600 s` to `60 s` at least 24 hours *before* a planned IP migration.

sections.content:
## The idea

DNS traffic routing turns hostname resolution from a static phonebook into a programmable, health-aware steering layer. When a client resolves `api.example.com`, the query traverses a **Stub Resolver** (OS/browser) to a **Recursive Resolver** (ISP, `1.1.1.1`, `8.8.8.8`), which walks the hierarchy—Root (`.`) → TLD (`.com`) → **Authoritative Nameserver**—and caches the answer for `TTL` seconds.

Modern authoritative DNS providers (Route 53, Cloudflare, NS1) evaluate **routing policies** dynamically at query time: **Latency/GeoDNS** inspects the client's IP (or EDNS Client Subnet `/24`) to pick the nearest region, **Health Checks** remove unreachable endpoints, and **Weighted Routing** distributes percentages across clusters. For sub-second responsiveness without DNS cache lag, global networks pair DNS with **Anycast BGP**, where dozens of edge POPs announce the exact same IP so internet routers steer packets to the closest POP automatically.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a user in Bengaluru (`103.21.58.44`) connecting to `api.example.com` (`TTL = 60 s`, Latency-Based + Failover policy across `ap-south-1` Mumbai and `ap-southeast-1` Singapore):

1. **Cache Check**: Chrome checks its local DNS cache and OS stub resolver; on a miss, it sends an `A` + `AAAA` query to its recursive resolver (`8.8.8.8`) over UDP/53 (or DoH/443).
2. **EDNS Client Subnet (ECS)**: On a recursive cache miss, `8.8.8.8` queries the authoritative nameserver for `example.com`, attaching `ECS = 103.21.58.0/24` (masking the last octet for privacy).
3. **Policy & Health Evaluation**: The authoritative server matches `103.21.58.0/24` to `ap-south-1` (`18 ms` RTT vs. `65 ms` to Singapore). It verifies that `ap-south-1`'s deep `/healthz` check (which tests DB connectivity) is `HEALTHY`.
4. **Response & Caching**: The authoritative server returns `A 13.234.10.5` with `TTL = 60`. `8.8.8.8` caches it for 60 s and returns it to Chrome.
5. **Regional Failover**: If `ap-south-1` fails 3 consecutive 30-second health checks, the authoritative server marks it `UNHEALTHY` and begins returning Singapore's IP (`54.169.22.8`). Existing users finish draining over 60–180 s as caches expire.

sections.content:
## Anycast BGP vs. DNS-based steering

Understanding the boundary between **Layer-3 Anycast BGP** and **Layer-7/DNS steering** is essential for global architectures:

- **Anycast BGP** assigns the *exact same IP address* (e.g., `1.1.1.1`) to servers in 200+ cities. Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) routers on the internet naturally forward packets along the shortest AS-path. If a POP goes offline, BGP withdraws its route announcement within seconds—requiring zero DNS TTL expiration.
- **DNS Steering** returns *different IP addresses* per region. It excels at directing traffic to distinct cloud regions (`us-east-1` vs. `eu-west-1`) without needing your own BGP ASN, and supports fine-grained weighted splits. Most large platforms combine both: DNS points to an Anycast CDN/edge, and the edge routes over private backbones to healthy regional origins.

## Comparing DNS routing policies

| Routing Policy | Selection Signal | Failover Speed | Best Use Case | Primary Caveat |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Weighted Round Robin** | Static percentage weights | 60–300 s (TTL-bound) | Multi-region canary / blue-green cuts | Skewed by large ISP resolver caches |
| **Latency-Based** | Measured RTT from client/ECS to region | 60–300 s (TTL-bound) | Global active-active SaaS | Inaccurate if resolver strips ECS |
| **Geolocation (GeoDNS)** | Country / continent / state mapping | 60–300 s (TTL-bound) | Data residency (GDPR), localized content | VPNs/proxies bypass true user country |
| **Active-Passive Failover** | Primary health check status | 90–300 s (3x30 s + TTL) | Disaster recovery to warm standby | Cold standby may fail under sudden 100% load |
| **Anycast BGP (Edge)** | Internet BGP AS-path topology | 1–10 s (BGP withdrawal) | Edge DDoS, CDN, global API frontends | Requires ASN + multi-POP network or CDN |

## Failure modes

- **Stale Resolver & Connection Pooling**: Even with `TTL = 30 s`, HTTP/2 and gRPC clients keep existing TCP connections open to the old IP for minutes or hours until a write fails. *Mitigation*: Pair DNS failover with server-side `GOAWAY` / connection max-age (`300 s`) and client-side retry on `UNAVAILABLE`.
- **Authoritative DNS Provider Outage**: If your single DNS provider suffers a control-plane or DDoS outage and your TTLs are 30 s, caches expire rapidly and your entire site becomes unreachable. *Mitigation*: Use dual-provider authoritative DNS (NS delegation across two vendors) or keep static records at 3600 s+.
- **Split-Horizon DNS Drift**: Internal VPCs resolve `api.example.com` to private IPs (`10.x.x.x`) while public DNS resolves to public IPs; out-of-sync changes break internal service calls. *Mitigation*: Manage both public and private hosted zones via unified Infrastructure-as-Code (Terraform/OpenTofu) with automated diff checks.
- **DNSSEC Misconfiguration**: Rotating keys without updating the parent zone's `DS` record causes validating resolvers (`8.8.8.8`, `1.1.1.1`) to return `SERVFAIL` globally. *Mitigation*: Use managed automated DNSSEC key rollovers and validate `DS` chains before cutover.

sections.eyebrow: 06 / Pre-migration TTL lowering and health-check design
sections.content:
## Pre-migration TTL lowering and health-check design

When migrating an IP or load balancer, lowering the TTL *at the moment of cutover* does nothing for clients that already cached the old `3600 s` record—they will continue hitting the old endpoint for up to an hour. Standard runbooks lower TTLs to `60 s` **at least 24 hours before** the migration, execute the IP swap, verify metrics, and raise the TTL back to `300–3600 s` afterward.

Similarly, DNS health checks must be **deep enough to catch real failures** (e.g., verifying local DB/cache reachability) without being **so brittle** that a transient downstream hiccup flaps DNS globally. Require `3` consecutive failures at `30 s` intervals before flipping a region unhealthy.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Lower record TTLs to `30–60 s` at least `24 hours` before any planned IP or load-balancer migration.
- [ ] Set the `SOA` minimum (negative caching) TTL to `60–300 s` so accidental `NXDOMAIN` responses recover quickly.
- [ ] Use `ALIAS` / `ANAME` / CNAME flattening at the zone apex (`example.com`) instead of invalid apex `CNAME` records.
- [ ] Configure JVM and long-lived HTTP/gRPC clients with explicit DNS cache TTLs (`30 s`) and connection max-age limits.
- [ ] Test regional failover regularly with chaos drills to verify standby capacity and health-check thresholds.

interviewProblems.title: DNS & Traffic Routing
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on DNS & Traffic Routing. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: DNS and traffic routing map human-readable hostnames to optimal, healthy server IPs using hierarchical caching, Anycast BGP, health checks, and geo/latency-aware policies.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Authoritative DNS applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Regional Edge / Anycast.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Regional Edge / Anycast experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Explicitly set `-Dsun.net.inetaddr.ttl=30` in JVM services, front origins with Anycast edge proxies, and keep old IPs draining gracefully.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: DNS is a pull-based, heavily cached control plane—even with a 30 s TTL, stubborn OS, browser, and JVM caches make instant DNS-only failover impossible without Anycast or edge proxies.
Avoid trap: Attempting to create a `CNAME` record at the root/apex domain (`example.com`), breaking `MX` and `NS` resolution instead of using `ALIAS`/`ANAME` flattening.
Avoid trap: Setting a `0 s` or `5 s` DNS TTL expecting instant failover, while ignoring ISP minimum-TTL clamping and browser connection pooling.
When to reach for it: Steering global users to the closest healthy regional load balancer via latency-based or GeoDNS policies.
When to reach for it: Performing gradual blue/green traffic shifts or weighted canary rollouts (e.g., 95% v1 / 5% v2) across independent clusters.

putItTogether.title: Putting Dns Traffic Routing Together
putItTogether.summary: DNS is a pull-based, heavily cached control plane—even with a 30 s TTL, stubborn OS, browser, and JVM caches make instant DNS-only failover impossible without Anycast or edge proxies.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Dns Traffic Routing before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: When `us-east-1` fails 3 consecutive health checks (90 s), Route 53 stops returning the US ALB IP and routes new DNS queries to `eu-west-1` while existing clients drain over 1–3 minutes.
